analysis.one_liner: Bars federal contracts for companies and their suppliers that violate child labor laws and refuse to fix it.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to punish federal contractors using illegal child labor cleared the Senate committee and sat on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never voted on it before the term ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal contractors and their subcontractors would have to disclose each year whether they have been cited, arbitrated, or sued for child labor violations in the past three years. Companies that violate child labor laws and refuse corrective action would go on an ineligible list and be barred from federal contracts for at least four years, and knowingly hiding violations would trigger False Claims Act penalties. A GAO study would document how widespread the problem is among federal contractors.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers working illegally in federal supply chains, who get a new enforcement tool aimed at their employers. Also taxpayers and law-abiding contractors who do not undercut rivals by using illegal child labor.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children working illegally in contractor supply chains

how_it_helps.text: Federal contractors must disclose annually, to the best of their knowledge, whether any final administrative determination, arbitration award, or civil judgment for a child labor violation was issued against them or their subcontractors in the past three years.

Companies with violations that fail to implement negotiated corrective measures go on an ineligible list, and agencies may not solicit offers from, award contracts to, or consent to subcontracts with them for a period set by the debarment official of no less than four years.
Knowingly failing to make the required disclosure is subject to False Claims Act penalties and referral for suspension and debarment proceedings.

The bill directs collected civil penalties from child labor cases to be used under the Fair Labor Standards Act, and requires a GAO study on the prevalence of child labor violations among federal contractors.

analysis.who_pays: Contractors and their subcontractors in labor-intensive federal work, who would bear disclosure, certification, and compliance costs, and could lose contract eligibility for at least four years if they violate child labor laws and refuse to correct them. The bill authorizes no additional funds, so the Labor Department must absorb the work with its existing budget.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes no additional funding, so the Labor Department must run the disclosure, list, debarment, and reporting regime with its existing budget.
Disclosures are made only to the best of the contractor's knowledge, so the system depends heavily on self-reporting rather than independent verification of child labor use.

Debarment is a severe sanction, and the bill reaches subcontractors and service providers a prime contractor may have limited visibility into; the bill mitigates this by requiring procedures consistent with the existing Federal Acquisition Regulation suspension and debarment process and by offering negotiated corrective measures before listing.
The bill covers only contractors tied to federal agencies, not child labor violations across the wider private economy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real: federal taxpayer dollars would no longer flow to companies that use illegal child labor and refuse to stop. The costs fall on the violating firms, which is the point, and on all contractors in modest compliance paperwork. The design is not airtight, since it leans on self-reporting and on the Labor Department doing more work with no new money, but it builds on existing procurement tools and offers a corrective path before debarment.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate's waiting list of business, but no senator ever called it up for a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the bill on October 26, 2023, joined by Republican Senator Josh Hawley.
The Senate referred it to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which ordered it reported favorably with an amendment in March 2024.
The committee, chaired by Senator Gary Peters, reported the bill with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on December 12, 2024, with written report 118-289.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 695 but never received a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
Only one of the 49 Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill beyond its original co-introducer.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal contractors that use or tolerate illegal child labor are better off, since they keep the contracts and face no new disclosure, corrective, or debarment consequences. Children in those supply chains are no better off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Contractors violating child labor laws, unchanged

industries.industry: Labor-intensive federal contractors (meatpacking sanitation, food processing, facilities services)
industries.note: These firms and their subcontractors would face annual disclosure of child labor violations, mandated corrective measures, and a ban of at least four years from federal contracts if they violate child labor laws and refuse to fix them. Their savings from illegal child labor come directly at the expense of the children involved.
Competitors that do not use illegal child labor gain when violators are barred from bidding, removing an unfair cost advantage. They also take on modest new certification and disclosure paperwork.
Agencies would gain a tool to keep violators out of the contractor pool, but must operate the new disclosure, referral, and reporting requirements with no additional appropriations.
